lesson_1.title: Greedy Selection: Largest First
task: A greedy algorithm makes the locally optimal choice at each stage. When maximizing a value, the optimal local choice is selecting the maximum available magnitude.
We will implement a greedy choice by sorting a dataset and extracting the largest element.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Logic: Compare (=, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥) | Logic: If / Else | Lists: Sorted Copy Of List (Built-in)
1. Define the function `greedy_largest(arr)`.
2. Execute an in-place sort on the array in descending order. This dictates an O(n log n) time complexity.
3. Evaluate if the array is empty. If true, return 0.
4. Return the first element from the sorted array, representing the maximum greedy choice.

lesson_1.title: Greedy Selection: Smallest First
task: Conversely, when minimizing a cost function, the optimal local choice is the element with the smallest magnitude.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Logic: Compare (=, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥) | Lists: Sorted Copy Of List (Built-in)
1. Define the function `greedy_smallest(arr)`.
2. Execute an in-place sort on the array in ascending order.
3. Evaluate the boundary: if the array is empty, return 0.
4. Return the first element from the array.

lesson_1.title: Greedy Aggregation: Top K Sum
task: To maximize a cumulative sum given a restricted number of selections (K), a greedy algorithm continuously selects the largest remaining elements.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Loops: Count With (For Loop) | Variables: Set Variable | Lists: Sorted Copy Of List (Built-in)
1. Define the function `greedy_sum(arr, k)`.
2. Sort the array in descending order to prioritize magnitude.
3. Initialize an accumulator variable to track the total sum.
4. Construct a loop constrained to iterate exactly K times. Ensure your loop bounds do not exceed the array length.
5. Inside the loop, accumulate the value of the current element into your total.
6. Return the accumulated total.

lesson_1.title: Greedy Minimization: Closest Number
task: Greedy choices can evaluate derived metrics, such as identifying an element that minimizes the absolute mathematical difference to a target.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Logic: Compare (=, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥) | Loops: For Each Item In List | Variables: Set Variable
1. Define the function `closest_number(arr, target)`.
2. Initialize tracking variables for the 'best match' and 'minimum difference', seeding them using the first element of the array.
3. Traverse the array. For each element, compute the absolute difference between it and the target.
4. If this newly computed difference is strictly less than your recorded minimum, update both tracking variables.
5. Return the best match.

lesson_1.title: Greedy Navigation: Minimum Cost Path
task: In navigation scenarios, a greedy strategy dictates moving to the adjacent node with the lowest immediate cost, disregarding potential future bottlenecks.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Variables: Set Variable | Math: Compound Assignment (+=, -=, *=, /=)
1. Define `greedy_path(costs)`. The parameter `costs` is an array of sub-arrays representing sequential choice sets.
2. Initialize an accumulator variable to track the total path cost.
3. Traverse the outer sequence of choice sets. For each set, identify the absolute minimum cost option available.
4. Increment your total cost by this selected minimum value.
5. Return the total cost. Observe that local optimization does not inherently guarantee global optimization.

lesson_2.title: Standard Denominations (Philippine Cashier)
task: The Coin Change Problem seeks to minimize the total number of coins dispensed. When utilizing standard currencies, a greedy algorithm successfully yields the optimal solution.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Lists: Create List With | Math: Remainder Of (Modulo) | Math: Advanced Math (//, **, >>, <<, &, |) | Variables: Set Variable
1. Define `ph_cashier(amount)`.
2. Initialize an array containing standard Philippine coin denominations in descending order.
3. Initialize a variable to track the total coins dispensed.
4. Iterate through the coin array. Utilize integer division to determine exactly how many times the current coin fits into the remaining amount.
5. Accumulate this count into your tracking variable.
6. Update the remaining amount using the modulo operator.
7. Return the finalized coin count.

lesson_2.title: Standard Denominations (US Cashier)
task: Applying the exact greedy methodology to a distinct currency system verifies the algorithm's interoperability with standard denomination structures.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Math: Remainder Of (Modulo)
1. Define `us_cashier(amount)`.
2. Initialize the US coin denominations in descending order.
3. Implement the identical greedy division and modulo iteration structure established in the previous activity.
4. Return the aggregated coin count.

lesson_2.title: Coin Breakdown Distribution
task: To provide operational transparency, the algorithm must record the specific denominations allocated rather than merely the total sum.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Lists: Create List With | Lists: Append To List | Math: Remainder Of (Modulo)
1. Define `coin_breakdown(amount, coins)`. Assume `coins` is provided in descending order.
2. Initialize an empty array to map the distribution.
3. Iterate through the available coins. Determine how many times the current coin fits into the remaining amount.
4. Append this specific integer count to your distribution array.
5. Reduce the remaining amount via modulo arithmetic.
6. Return the distribution array to map the exact subset allocation.

lesson_2.title: Arbitrary Currency System
task: A robust greedy algorithm must self-organize the dataset prior to execution. If a currency system is provided unsorted, the algorithm must execute an O(n log n) preprocessing phase.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Math: Remainder Of (Modulo) | Lists: Sorted Copy Of List (Built-in)
1. Define `custom_change(amount, coins)`.
2. Execute an in-place descending sort on the `coins` array.
3. Apply the standard iterative division and modulo reduction logic.
4. Return the aggregated coin count.

lesson_2.title: Exact Change Validation
task: The Greedy Choice Property is not mathematically flawless. If an arbitrary coin system lacks a 1-unit denomination, the greedy algorithm may fail to process the exact amount.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Math: Remainder Of (Modulo) | Lists: Sorted Copy Of List (Built-in)
1. Define `can_make_change(amount, coins)`.
2. Sort the array of coins in descending order.
3. Execute the greedy subtraction and modulo logic to iteratively reduce the target amount.
4. Evaluate the terminal state: if the remaining amount has been reduced exactly to zero, return True.
5. If a non-zero remainder exists, the greedy constraints failed. Return False.

lesson_3.title: Activity Preprocessing (Sorting by End Time)
task: The Activity Selection algorithm maximizes concurrent scheduling by unconditionally prioritizing tasks that terminate the earliest.
To achieve O(n log n) efficiency, the dataset must be sorted utilizing the termination boundaries.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Lists: Sorted Copy Of List (Built-in)
1. Define `sort_by_end(activities)`. Assume `activities` is a 2D array where each sub-array contains a start time and an end time.
2. Utilize the sorting construct to arrange the array in ascending order based specifically on the element representing the end time.
3. Return the sorted 2D array structure.

lesson_3.title: The Event Scheduler
task: Upon structural preprocessing, a single O(n) linear sweep is sufficient to greedily aggregate compatible activities.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Logic: Compare (=, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥) | Variables: Set Variable | Math: Compound Assignment (+=, -=, *=, /=)
1. Define `schedule_events(activities)`. Ensure boundary validation: if the array is empty, return 0.
2. Assume the input is already sorted by end time. Initialize your event count to 1, and set your tracking variable to the termination time of the initial event.
3. Iterate through the array starting from the second event.
4. Evaluate overlap: if the start time of the current activity is greater than or equal to your tracked end time, the event is compatible.
5. When an event is compatible, increment your count and update the tracked end time to the termination time of the newly scheduled event.
6. Return the total count.

lesson_3.title: Algorithmic Conflict Detection
task: Evaluating sequence validity requires an algorithm capable of detecting structural overlap between continuous states.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Logic: Compare (=, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥) | Loops: Count With (For Loop)
1. Define `has_conflicts(activities)`. Assume the array is sorted by start time.
2. Construct an iteration loop that safely evaluates adjacent pairs without triggering an out-of-bounds error.
3. Evaluate the boundary violation: if the end time of the current activity strictly exceeds the start time of the subsequent activity, a conflict exists.
4. If a conflict is detected, return True immediately.
5. Return False if the sequential scan verifies all activities are perfectly disjoint.

lesson_3.title: Aggregating Scheduled Duration
task: To determine the operational efficiency of the scheduled blocks, the algorithm must dynamically map and aggregate the structural differences.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Variables: Set Variable | Math: Compound Assignment (+=, -=, *=, /=) | Lists: Create List With
1. Define `total_duration(activities)`.
2. Initialize an accumulator variable to track total time.
3. Iterate through the multi-dimensional array.
4. Compute the mathematical duration of the current task by subtracting its start time from its end time.
5. Increment your tracking variable by this computed magnitude.
6. Return the accumulated total.

lesson_3.title: Facility Allocation (Max Overlap)
task: Determining the minimum number of rooms required to host all events requires tracking the maximum state of concurrency.
Instructions:
Blocks you'll need: Functions: Define Function (With Return) | Math: Compound Assignment (+=, -=, *=, /=) | Lists: Sorted Copy Of List (Built-in)
1. Define `rooms_required(activities)`.
2. Isolate two distinct mathematical sequences: an array of start times and an array of end times. Sort both in ascending order.
3. Initialize boundary pointers for both arrays, alongside variables tracking current rooms and the maximum recorded rooms.

4. Traverse the sequences: if the current start time occurs strictly before the current end time, a new room is needed. Increment the current room count, advance the start pointer, and update the recorded maximum.
5. Otherwise, a room has freed up. Decrement the current room count and advance the end pointer.
6. Return the maximum recorded rooms.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: Pre-Sorting Over Exhaustive Search
task: Repeatedly searching an array for the largest remaining value results in O(n²) time complexity. Sorting the data first allows you to extract the largest values efficiently.
Optimization Guidelines:
Blocks you'll need: Loops: Count With (For Loop) | Lists: Sorted Copy Of List (Built-in)
1. Eliminate the nested loops used to find the maximum value.
2. Sort the array in descending order before starting the iteration.
3. Create a single loop that iterates exactly K times.
4. Accumulate the values from the beginning of the sorted array.
5. Return the total to achieve an O(n log n) time complexity.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: Constant Time Modulo Deduction
task: Using a loop to repeatedly subtract coin values simulates an inefficient linear search. Mathematical division and modulo operations can process this in constant time per coin.
Optimization Guidelines:
Blocks you'll need: Math: Remainder Of (Modulo) | Math: Advanced Math (//, **, >>, <<, &, |) | Loops: Count With (For Loop)
1. Remove the inner loop that handles repeated subtraction.
2. Use integer division to determine how many times the current coin fits into the remaining amount.
3. Add the division result to your total coin counter.
4. Use the modulo operator to update the remaining amount.
5. Removing the inner loop produces a more efficient algorithm.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: Greedy Activity Scheduling
task: Evaluating every combination of activities takes exponential time. Sorting the activities by their end times allows for a single-pass greedy selection.
Optimization Guidelines:
Blocks you'll need: Lists: Sorted Copy Of List (Built-in) | Loops: Count With (For Loop) | Logic: If / Else
1. Sort the given activities based on their termination times.
2. Track the end time of the most recently selected activity. Start with the first activity in the sorted list.
3. Iterate through the remaining activities sequentially.
4. If an activity starts at or after the tracked end time, select it and update the tracked end time.
5. Return the total number of selected activities to observe an O(n log n) efficiency.
